milestones.title: First mention in the chronicles
milestones.detail: Moscow is first recorded in 1147 as the place where Yuri Dolgorukiy met Sviatoslav Olgovich. It was then a minor town on the western border of Rostov-Suzdal.

milestones.title: First Kremlin walls (1150s)
milestones.detail: The town was turned into a fortified stronghold in the 1150s, when the first walls of the Kremlin were built.

milestones.title: Sacked in the Mongol invasion
milestones.detail: During the Mongol invasions of 1237-1238 Moscow was sacked after the destruction of Ryazan.

milestones.title: Daniel becomes the first prince of Moscow
milestones.detail: Daniel, youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, received Moscow as hereditary land and founded its line of princes, the start of the Grand Principality of Moscow.

milestones.title: Brick Kremlin walls completed
milestones.detail: Italian architects, among them Pietro Antonio Solari and Marco Ruffo, rebuilt the Kremlin under Ivan III. The present walls, designed by Solari, were completed in 1495.

milestones.title: Tsardom proclaimed; great fire
milestones.detail: The Tsardom of Russia was proclaimed in 1547 with Moscow as its centre. Fires destroyed much of the town the same year.

milestones.title: Crimean Tatars burn the city
milestones.detail: In 1571 the Crimean Tatars captured Moscow and burned everything except the Kremlin.

milestones.title: Polish-Lithuanian occupation ended
milestones.detail: Troops of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth held Moscow from 1610 until 1612, when forces from Nizhny Novgorod and other Russian cities, led by Dmitry Pozharsky and Kuzma Minin, besieged the Kremlin and expelled them.

milestones.title: Capital moved to Saint Petersburg
milestones.detail: Peter the Great moved his government to the newly built Saint Petersburg in 1712, and Moscow's importance declined through the imperial period.

milestones.title: Napoleon's occupation and the fire of Moscow
milestones.detail: Muscovites were evacuated when Napoleon invaded in 1812 and the city burned. Streets such as the Arbat were destroyed and rebuilt in the early 19th century.

milestones.title: Capital returns to Moscow
milestones.detail: The Soviet government moved the capital back to Moscow on 12 March 1918.
milestones.source: Presidential Library, 'Moscow becomes the capital of the Soviet State', https://www.prlib.ru/en/history/619089 , via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow

milestones.title: Moscow Metro opens
milestones.detail: The Metro started operating in 1935 and quickly became the centrepiece of the city's transport.

milestones.title: Battle of Moscow
milestones.detail: Between October 1941 and January 1942 the German Army Group Centre was stopped at the outskirts of the city and then pushed back. Many factories and much of the government were evacuated.

milestones.title: Ring road becomes the city boundary
milestones.detail: The 109 km Moscow Ring Road (MKAD) opened in 1961 and marked the city's administrative boundary until suburbs beyond it were incorporated in the 1980s.

milestones.title: Summer Olympic Games
milestones.detail: Moscow hosted the 1980 Summer Olympics, which the United States and other Western countries boycotted.

milestones.title: New Moscow more than doubles the city's area
milestones.detail: On 1 July 2012 territory to the south-west was annexed from Moscow Oblast, raising the city's area from 1,091 to 2,511 square kilometres and adding about 233,000 people.

landmarks.name: Ivan the Great Bell Tower
landmarks.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_the_Great_Bell_Tower (height 81 m; first built 1505-1508); https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Колокольня_Ивана_Великого (raised to 81 m in 1599-1600)
landmarks.note: Built 1505-1508 at about 60 m and raised to its present height in 1600 under Boris Godunov. Source added at verification: the English article gives only the 1508 completion and the 81 m height; the Russian article describes the 1599-1600 superstructure and its inscription dated 7108 (1600). Values unchanged.

landmarks.name: Spasskaya Tower (Kremlin)
landmarks.note: Gate tower built in 1491; the hipped roof that gives the present height was added in 1624-1625. The 71 m includes the star.

landmarks.name: Shukhov Radio Tower
landmarks.note: Height of the hyperboloid structure as built (the design was cut from 350 m).

landmarks.name: Cathedral of Christ the Saviour (rebuilt)
landmarks.note: Height to the top cross. The 19th-century original on the site was dynamited on 5 December 1931; the rebuilt cathedral was consecrated on 19 August 2000.

notes: Start date: 1147 is the first mention of Moscow in the chronicles and is the standard, uncontested date; the settlement itself is older but undated in the sources consulted, and the first fortification is put only in 'the 1150s' (entered as 1150, estimated). Population: there is no figure before 1343, so the app should show no reliable estimate for the first two centuries. Figures to 1850 are Chandler's estimates and are uncertain before about 1700 (his 1570 and 1575 values bracket the 1571 destruction; English Wikipedia cites annals that imply a much larger city before 1571). The 1897, 1926 and 1939 points are taken directly from census tables on Demoscope. The 1813, 1871, 1882, 1902, 1912, 1917, 1920 and 1931 points come from the population table on Russian Wikipedia, whose early entries rest on a web encyclopedia and Soviet handbooks that were not checked individually; several are rounded to hundreds there. English Wikipedia's census table gives slightly different values for 1897 (1,038,625) and 1939 (4,141,633) and 1,995,252 for 1926; the Demoscope figures were preferred. All figures are for the city within its boundaries of the time, which expanded repeatedly. Chandler's 1875, 1900, 1914 and 1925 estimates were dropped in favour of the counts. Landmarks: no sourced height was found for the Kremlin's Dormition Cathedral or the Sukharev Tower (1701, demolished 1934), and no completion year for the 72 m Novodevichy Convent bell tower, so they are omitted. The original Cathedral of Christ the Saviour (demolished 1931) is not entered separately because no height for the original was found. The Ivan the Great Bell Tower and Spasskaya Tower are dated to the year they reached their present height, not first construction. Stalin-era and modern towers use CTBUH heights and years; CTBUH gives 239 m for the Moscow State University building. Ostankino Tower's height is from Wikipedia.
